USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the proposed Section 301 $50 billion list as leverage through the May comment and hearing process, but do not implement it yet and do not proceed with the additional $100 billion tranche floated on April 5. Open a structured negotiation aimed at forced technology transfer, discriminatory licensing, and a measurable goods-deficit reduction, while making clear that China’s $50 billion soy/auto/aircraft list will be matched if Beijing implements first. Use the two-month procedural window to convert pressure into commitments rather than locking in a tariff spiral that hits the farm belt before any structural gain is in hand.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild opportunity, not a danger, because the United States still holds the initiative and the real economy is not yet paying a material price. The Section 301 record (2017-08-14 investigation; 2018-03-22 findings and memorandum; 2018-04-03 proposed list of about 1300 lines / $50B aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery) documents unresolved IP and Made-in-China-2025 practices after the November 2017 Beijing visit produced only commercial MOUs and no structural concessions. US macro as of early April remains expansionary: industrial production 103.3 (up about 2 percent in the window), Michigan sentiment 98.8, funds rate 1.69 percent, 10-year 2.79 percent, broad dollar easier not tighter. Bilateral goods still run a large imbalance (IMPCH about $38.2B vs EXPCH about $10.5B in the latest month; BOPGTB about -$71B), which is leverage, not vulnerability. China industry, reserves (about $3.14T) and merchandise exports are also intact, so this is not a distressed opponent — but it is more export-exposed to the US market than the reverse.

The offsetting costs that keep the score near zero rather than a large opportunity are real and already visible. On 2018-04-02 China implemented about $3B of 232 retaliation (pork, fruit, nuts, wine). On 2018-04-04 it proposed 25 percent duties on about $50B of US goods, ranking soybeans first (about $12–14B; about one-third of the US crop; about 40 percent of China soybean imports), plus autos and some aircraft, and said timing depends on what Washington does. Soy futures fell 3 to 5 percent the day of the announcement; the American Soybean Association put one-morning mark-to-market losses near $1.72B and called the hit devastating. Farm-state Republicans (Ernst, Fischer, Bacon) and USDA Perdue immediately flagged political and income risk in a sector already facing weak farm income. VIX remains about 20 (about double last fall) and jumped above 23 around the 301 rollout. Those are concentrated export and political threats, not a GDP or financial-stability event.

That combination justifies negotiate at action_score 0, not further tariff escalation and not rollback. Further escalation (the April 5 instruction to study another $100B) would likely bring implementation of China soy list, deepen farm-belt losses, and raise input-cost risk on the US 301 machinery/ICT lines before comments close (written comments to May 11; hearing May 15). Rollback or purchase concessions would abandon the 301 finding with no Chinese offer on the table. Mnuchin and Kudlow have already described parallel talks (deficit cut on the order of $100B, end forced JVs/tech transfer) and Chinese Vice Finance Minister Zhu publicly asked Washington to work in a constructive manner while warning Beijing will not simply back down. Hold the published $50B list, keep the WTO licensing case, and bargain in the comment window.
key_factors: Section 301 $50B list published but not in force; comment/hearing window through mid-May
China mirrored with a proposed $50B list concentrated on soybeans, autos, and aircraft, plus $3B of already-implemented 232 retaliation
US real economy still firm (rising IP, high sentiment, contained inflation); dispute not yet a macro shock
Large bilateral goods imbalance remains US leverage; China more dependent on the US goods market
Farm-belt mark-to-market losses and GOP-state political pressure are the main US cost of further escalation
Informal talks are open (Mnuchin/Kudlow; Zhu) but no structural Chinese offer exists yet
April 5 $100B escalation threat raises spiral risk without improving negotiating terms

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump visits Beijing; large package of commercial deals announced (many MOUs). No substantive concessions on structural IP / tech-transfer issues.

USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
China imposes retaliatory tariffs on about $3B of US goods (pork, fruit, nuts, wine, and related items) in response to Section 232 steel/aluminum tariffs.
USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery and related sectors. Public comment process opens.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
US industrial production latest 103.3329 (2018-04-01), up about 2% in the lookback window.
Michigan consumer sentiment 98.8 in April 2018 after 101.4 in March — still high, modest dip only.
US goods imports from China latest ~$38.2B vs US exports to China ~$10.5B (EXPCH), preserving a large bilateral imbalance.
VIX 20.24 on 2018-04-11, roughly double October 2017 levels; spiked above 23 around the late-March/early-April 301 sequence.
China reserves excluding gold still ~$3.14T in April 2018 — no FX/reserve stress visible.

USTR April 3, 2018: proposed list targets products that benefit from Chinese industrial plans including Made in China 2025; ~1,300 tariff lines; public notice-and-comment and a hearing before any final determination.

China buys about $14B of US soybeans a year — nearly a third of the US crop; soybean prices tumbled 3 to 5% on the news; China list of 106 items concentrates pain on farm and politically sensitive goods.

China gave no date for the 25% hike and said it depends on what Trump does; Iowa Soybean Association expected Brazil substitution and market disruption; Zhu Guangyao asked Washington to work constructively and warned Beijing would not back down under pressure.

ASA: China takes 61% of US soybean exports; futures down nearly 40 cents; estimated $1.72B of crop value lost the morning of the announcement; China said its 25% tariff takes effect based on US action.
Mnuchin: talks underway to cut the bilateral deficit by $100B and eliminate forced JVs/tech transfer; tariffs not on hold unless the president signs an acceptable agreement.
April 5: Trump instructed USTR to consider tariffs on an additional $100B of Chinese goods after China $50B list, while saying talks on technology and IP could continue.
Section 301 hearing set for May 15, 2018; appear-by date April 23; comments on product coverage and whether duties would harm US interests.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the 4 April matching list as contingent leverage and do not add a new tariff tranche now. Use the USTR comment window (into late May) and the existing Liu He–Mnuchin channel to talk without new structural or purchase commitments, while pressing the WTO case and making clear that our $50B list fires only if Washington implements Section 301. Further unilateral escalation would invite the additional $100B envelope Trump just ordered USTR to study, which we cannot match on a like-for-like goods basis.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not yet existential. On 3 April USTR published a proposed 25% list on ~1,300 lines/~$50B aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and machinery — explicitly products that benefit from industrial plans including Made in China 2025 — plus a WTO case and forthcoming investment restrictions (timeline 2018-04-03; USTR 3 April release). That is a direct hit on the upgrading strategy, not a consumer-goods slap. China has already answered: live 232 retaliation on ~$3B (2018-04-02) and a proposed 25% list on ~$50B of soybeans, autos, chemicals and aircraft (2018-04-04). Neither $50B list is in force; Lighthizer said no duties until the comment/hearing process finishes. The real-economy read is still calm: China IP ~7% y/y, merchandise exports still expanding, reserves ~$3.14T, discount rate unchanged at 2.9%, and CNY stronger (DEXCHUS 6.27 on 11 April vs ~6.59 in mid-October). That keeps the score below the +0.5 ‘major sectors already hit / FX pressure’ anchor. What lifts it above neutral is the 5 April Trump instruction to consider another $100B of 301 tariffs after our match, plus the arithmetic that $50B is only about one-ninth of US imports from China versus about one-third of our US imports — Washington has more tariff room. Action stays at 0/negotiate rather than escalate or concede: Zhu Guangyao already said we do not want a trade war and will not yield to external pressure; talks exist but have produced little; purchase/structural concessions are premature while the US has not made a matching offer and is still expanding threats. A second Chinese tariff wave now would likely harden the $100B track and raise unemployment risk in export hubs without forcing IP/MIC-2025 off the US list.
key_factors: USTR $50B list targets MIC 2025 sectors (aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery) but is still in a public-comment process
China already matched dollar-for-dollar ($3B live 232 retaliation + $50B proposed 301 list on soy, autos, aircraft)
Trump 5 April instruction to study an additional $100B shows the US will escalate if we keep adding tariffs
US has more tariff ammunition (bilateral import asymmetry); further escalation is a losing volume game
China macros not yet bitten: IP ~7% y/y, reserves ~$3.14T, CNY firmer, policy rate unchanged
Liu He–Mnuchin channel and WTO filings exist; talks have not produced a deal worth buying
